title: Muscular System
shortDescription: The three muscle types and the major labelled skeletal muscles that move the body.
genZNote: Muscles don't push — they only pull. Every movement is a contraction working against something.

illustration.alt: Labelled illustration of the major muscles of the human body
illustration.caption: Muscular System — Cellfie Human Anatomy

structures.name: Sternocleidomastoid
structures.description: Muscle running along the side of the neck.

structures.name: Pectoralis major
structures.function: Moves the shoulder joint; flexes and rotates the arm.

structures.name: Biceps brachii
structures.description: Muscle on the front of the upper arm.
structures.function: Flexes the elbow and rotates the forearm.

structures.name: Rectus abdominis
structures.description: Vertical muscle running down the front of the abdomen.
structures.function: Flexes the trunk; supports posture (the “six-pack” muscle).

structures.name: Quadriceps femoris
structures.description: Group of four muscles on the front of the thigh.

structures.name: Hamstrings
structures.description: Group of muscles on the back of the thigh.
structures.function: Flexes the knee and extends the hip.

structures.name: Gastrocnemius
structures.function: Plantar-flexes the foot (points the toes down), powers walking and jumping.

comparisons.distinction: Skeletal muscle is voluntary and attached to bone (movement); smooth muscle is involuntary and lines internal organs and vessels.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary and attaches to bone; cardiac muscle is involuntary and found only in the heart.
A tendon is the tough connective-tissue cord that anchors a muscle to bone; the muscle itself is the contractile tissue that generates movement.

questions.prompt: In the labelled muscular illustration, which muscle group is on the front of the thigh and extends the knee?
questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris sits on the front of the thigh and extends the knee; the hamstrings, on the back of the thigh, do the opposite (flex the knee).
optionNotes: On the back of the thigh, flexes rather than extends the knee.
A calf muscle, not a thigh muscle.
A shoulder muscle, unrelated to the knee.

questions.prompt: Which muscle type is involuntary and found only in the heart?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is involuntary and unique to the heart. Smooth muscle is also involuntary but is found in organs and vessels, not the heart.
optionNotes: Involuntary, but found in organs/vessels, not the heart specifically.

questions.prompt: True or False: Smooth muscle is under voluntary control.
questions.explanation: False — smooth muscle (found in organs like the stomach and blood vessels) is involuntary, unlike skeletal muscle.

sections.heading: Major Labelled Muscles
bullets: Sternocleidomastoid — neck, rotates and flexes the head.
Deltoid — shoulder, lifts and rotates the arm.
Pectoralis major — chest, moves the arm across the body.
Biceps brachii — front of upper arm, flexes the elbow.
Rectus abdominis — abdomen ("the abs"), flexes the trunk.
External oblique — side of abdomen, rotates and bends the trunk.
Quadriceps femoris — front of thigh, extends the knee.
Hamstrings — back of thigh, flexes the knee.
Gastrocnemius — calf, points the foot downward (plantarflexion).

sections.heading: The Three Types of Muscle Tissue

rows: Attached to bones via tendons; produces body movement
Walls of internal organs (stomach, intestines, blood vessels)
Heart wall only; contracts rhythmically without conscious control

sections.heading: Muscle Contraction and Tendons
sections.body: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons (tough, fibrous connective tissue). Muscles can only pull, never push — they contract to move a bone at a joint, then rely on an opposing muscle to move the bone back the other way (an antagonistic pair, e.g. biceps and triceps).

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: The muscular system produces movement through contraction, using three muscle types: skeletal (voluntary), smooth (involuntary, organ walls), and cardiac (involuntary, heart only).
keyFacts: Only skeletal muscle is under voluntary/conscious control.
Cardiac muscle is found exclusively in the heart wall.
Muscles connect to bone via tendons, not ligaments (ligaments connect bone to bone).
Muscles work in antagonistic pairs since they can only pull, not push.
commonConfusion: Tendons (muscle-to-bone) are commonly confused with ligaments (bone-to-bone).

Smooth muscle (organ walls, involuntary) is sometimes confused with skeletal muscle simply because both can be described as "striated" vs "non-striated" incorrectly — only skeletal and cardiac muscle are striated; smooth muscle is not.

highYieldFacts: Cardiac muscle is the only muscle type found solely in one organ — the heart.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary; smooth and cardiac muscle are both involuntary.
commonTraps: Don't say muscles can "push" bones — they only contract and pull; opposing muscles are needed to reverse a movement.
Tendon vs. ligament: tendon = muscle-to-bone, ligament = bone-to-bone. This pairing is heavily tested.
mustRemember: Three muscle types: skeletal (voluntary), smooth (involuntary, organs), cardiac (involuntary, heart).
Muscles attach to bone via tendons and act in antagonistic pairs.

confusedTerms.distinction: A tendon connects muscle to bone; a ligament connects bone to bone at a joint.
